outcome: Still open as of 11 Oct 2026: no source I read reports any irrational algebraic number shown normal in any base, nor a counterexample. Since 26 Jan 2024 the in-window events are a zeta-function criterion for normality of algebraic numbers (Kanado and Saito, Dec 2024, equivalence only), five neighbouring normal-number papers that concern different questions, and a formal-statement issue in the DeepMind formal-conjectures repository (Feb to Aug 2026) with no new mathematics. Earlier events are partial bounds on digit counts and a 2005 to 2018 line of claims that square roots of non-squares, and sqrt(2), are normal in base 2; no third-party acceptance of those claims was found.
problem_asks: Statement: 'Are all irrational algebraic numbers normal?' Parts: (1) the quantifier: every real irrational algebraic number alpha (irrational and algebraic over the rationals). (2) the property: 'normal', which the statement leaves unqualified. Two readings are both live and the statement does not choose between them: (a) normal in some integer base b >= 2, i.e. every block of k digits appears with frequency b^-k in base b; (b) absolutely normal, i.e. normal in every integer base b >= 2 at once, the form in which Borel's 1950 proposal is usually quoted. (b) implies (a); the converse is not automatic. The Wikipedia article as fetched on 2 Oct 2026 defines 'normal' as 'normal in all integer bases greater than or equal to 2 (sometimes called absolutely normal)', which favours reading (b) for this bullet. (3) The statement names no base and no particular number, so a result for one base, or for one family of numbers, answers part (2) only in that restricted form. The statement asks for nothing else: not simple normality, not digit-count bounds, not a specific constant.

events.what_happened: Bailey, Borwein, Crandall and Pomerance, 'On the binary expansions of algebraic numbers', J. Theorie des Nombres de Bordeaux 16 (2004) 487-518. Central result (abstract, verbatim in parts): if a real y has algebraic degree D > 1, the number of 1-bits among the first N binary digits of |y| satisfies > C N^(1/D) for a constant C depending on y and sufficiently large N. Applications: transcendence of sums of 2^(-f(n)) for fast-growing f, and re-proof of transcendence of the Kempner-Mahler number. Notes the bound is not a statement about digit frequencies.
events.revisions: Journal version only (JTNB 16(3)). No earlier preprint was looked for on arXiv, so the year is the journal year and may be earlier than the first public written argument.
events.delivers: A lower bound of order N^(1/D) on the count of binary 1s in any irrational algebraic number of degree D. This is a sublinear count bound. It gives no digit frequency, so by itself it does not establish even simple normality to base 2 of any number; Kanado and Saito (arXiv 2412.02337, section 1) state that these lower bounds 'do not verify the simple normality of alpha to base 2'.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no base is shown normal for any algebraic irrational, and the digit count is not shown to have frequency 1/2.

checked_by.who: Journal de Theorie des Nombres de Bordeaux (refereed number theory journal)
checked_by.qualification: Refereed research journal in number theory; the refereeing reports were not inspected
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in vol. 16 (2004), issue 3

events.direction: A partial result pointing the way normality would predict (algebraic irrationals cannot have very few 1s), but the quantity it bounds is a count, not a frequency, so it does not move the normality question in the direction of a proof.

events.what_happened: Boris Adamczewski and Yann Bugeaud, 'On the complexity of algebraic numbers I. Expansions in integer bases', arXiv math/0511674 (28 Nov 2005), published Ann. of Math. (2) 165 (2007) 547-565. Abstract (verbatim in parts): 'We prove that the b-adic expansion of every irrational algebraic number cannot have low complexity.' Also: irrational automatic and morphic numbers are transcendental.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only (28 Nov 2005); journal version Ann. of Math. 2007.
events.delivers: A lower bound on the complexity (subword-counting function) of the base-b expansion of every irrational algebraic number, in the sense 'cannot have low complexity'. Normal numbers have maximal complexity in every base, so this is a constraint in the same direction as normality, but it is about complexity, not about digit frequencies, and it establishes normality of no number.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no algebraic irrational is shown normal in any base, and no frequency statement is made.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record in mathematics
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, Ann. of Math. (2) 165 (2007), no. 2, 547-565

events.direction: Partial constraint consistent with normality; a different property (complexity) from the one the problem names; does not settle any part of problem_asks.

events.what_happened: Richard Isaac, 'On the simple normality to base 2 of the square root of s, for s not a perfect square', arXiv math/0512404. Claims each number sqrt(s), s not a perfect square, is simply normal to base 2 (frequency of digit 1 tends to 1/2). Method: elementary ideas from the calculus of finite differences. The v2 comment (21 Sep 2006) states 'Lemma 6 of the original version is incorrect' and gives an alternative argument; the two versions agree through Lemma 4.
events.revisions: v1 16 Dec 2005; v2 21 Sep 2006 (v2 comment: Lemma 6 of v1 incorrect; alternative argument for the same result).
events.delivers: Simple normality to base 2 (not full normality in base 2, and no other base) for the infinite family sqrt(s), s a positive non-square integer. Restricted in base, in notion of normality, and in family: it does not cover other quadratic irrationals such as 1+sqrt(2), or any algebraic irrational of degree 3 or more.
events.remains: Full normality in base 2; normality in any other base; normality in some base or absolute normality for any algebraic irrational outside the sqrt(s) family.
events.doubts: MathWorld's Normal Number entry (last updated 2 Oct 2026, as fetched) says: 'this work uses a nonstandard approach that appears rather cloudy to at least some experts who have looked at it.' The experts are not named and no review is cited. The v2 comment itself concedes an error in Lemma 6 of v1. The arXiv abstract page shows no journal reference, and I found no journal publication.
events.direction: Claims a restricted case in favour of the conjecture: one base (base 2), simple normality only, and one family of algebraic irrationals (square roots of non-squares). Whether the argument holds is unresolved in the sources read.

events.what_happened: Richard Isaac, 'On a sufficient condition that the square root of s is simply normal to base 2, for s not a perfect square', arXiv 1104.1616 (8 Apr 2011, single version). Abstract (verbatim in parts): 'A simple proof is given of a sufficient condition that the square root of s is simply normal to base 2, for s not a perfect square. This relates to previous work of the author.' The condition is not named in the abstract as fetched.
events.delivers: A simpler proof of a sufficient condition for simple normality to base 2 of sqrt(s). It is conditional on that sufficient condition and has the same restricted scope as the 2005 claim: base 2, simple normality, square roots of non-squares.
events.remains: Full normality, all other bases, all other algebraic irrationals, as for the 2005 entry.
events.doubts: Same author as the 2005 and 2013 claims; no third-party reading of this paper found. The sufficient condition is not restated in the abstract, so its validity rests on the paper body, which I did not read.
events.direction: Same as the 2005 claim: a restricted case in favour of the conjecture, with the restriction unchanged.

events.what_happened: Richard Isaac, 'A proof that the square root of s for s not a perfect square is simply normal to base 2', arXiv 1309.0666. Abstract (verbatim in parts): 'an open problem has been whether simple irrationals like square root of 2 are normal to any base. We show that each number of the form square root of s for s not a perfect square is simply normal to base 2 ... The proof is mostly elementary and self contained but some basic probability is used.' Main idea: the tails of an expansion. Versions: v1 3 Sep 2013; v2 10 Jun 2015; v3 20 Jul 2016; v4 20 Dec 2016; v5 19 Sep 2018, which 'rewrote Section 2.3 and corrected the probability sample space used in the previous version' (v5 comment).
events.revisions: v1 3 Sep 2013; v2 10 Jun 2015; v3 20 Jul 2016; v4 20 Dec 2016; v5 19 Sep 2018 (corrected the probability sample space used in earlier versions).
events.delivers: The same restricted claim as the 2005 entry: simple normality to base 2 of sqrt(s), s a non-square positive integer, by a different argument. No other base; no full normality; no other family of algebraic irrationals.
events.remains: Full normality in base 2; every other base; normality for every other algebraic irrational.
events.doubts: The author's own v5 comment reports that the probability sample space used in v1 to v4 was wrong, so the earlier versions of this argument were corrected once. No journal reference is listed on the arXiv page. The doubt that MathWorld expresses (see the 2005 entry) concerns the 2005 preprint and is not stated about this one; I did not read the body to judge the 2013 proof.
events.direction: Claims a restricted case in favour of the conjecture by a different argument from the 2005 claim.

events.what_happened: Tanguy Rivoal, 'On the bits counting function of real numbers', J. Australian Math. Soc. 85 (2008) 95-111. From a search excerpt of the Cambridge abstract, not opened: gives a slight refinement of the Bailey-Borwein-Crandall-Pomerance 2004 lower bound for the number of binary 1s of an irrational algebraic number; also inequalities relating the counting function for x+y, xy and 1/x.
events.delivers: A refined lower bound on the binary 1-count of irrational algebraic numbers. Same type as the 2004 entry: a sublinear count with no digit frequency. Refinement constant not retrieved.

checked_by.who: Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, vol. 85 (2008), pp. 95-111 (per search excerpt)

events.direction: Partial result of the same kind as the 2004 bound; no move toward normality beyond a sharper count.

events.what_happened: Hajime Kaneko, 'On the binary digits of algebraic numbers', J. Australian Math. Soc. 89 (2010) 233-244 (received Jan 2010, accepted June 2010). From a search excerpt, not opened: lower bounds on the number of digit changes (0 to 1 transitions) in the binary expansion of algebraic irrationals; for 1/sqrt(3) an explicit bound of order sqrt(N).
events.delivers: Lower bounds on binary digit changes for algebraic irrationals (explicit for 1/sqrt(3)). Counts transitions, not frequencies; establishes normality of no number.

checked_by.who: Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society (refereed journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, vol. 89 (2010), pp. 233-244 (per search excerpt)

events.direction: Partial result about digit transitions, not frequencies; no move toward normality beyond a lower bound on a different count.

events.what_happened: Johan Sejr Brinch Nielsen and Jakob Grue Simonsen, 'An experimental investigation of the normality of irrational algebraic numbers', Math. Comp. 82 (2013) 1837-1858, published electronically 20 Mar 2013. From the search excerpt of the AMS abstract, not opened: 121 algebraic irrationals (Pisot-Vijayaraghavan, Salem, square roots of non-squares, random ones), 2*3^18 binary digits each, tested with generalized serial statistics and a maximum relative frequency deviation test in bases 2, 3, 5, 7, 10 for block sizes 1 to 4. All 121 passed in all those bases for block sizes 1 to 4; 92 passed every test up to block size 4. The authors describe the data as suggesting an empirical base for Borel's conjecture.
events.revisions: No earlier preprint was looked for; the date is the electronic publication date in Math. Comp.
events.delivers: A finite numerical check on 121 specific algebraic irrationals, to block size 4 in five bases. Under section 2.1 this is finitely many instances of a claim about all algebraic irrationals; it establishes no normality for any number and does not move any quantity the statement names.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, vol. 82, issue 283 (per search excerpt)

events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture (no counterexample among the 121 numbers tested); not a proof and not a move toward one.

events.what_happened: Yuya Kanado and Kota Saito, 'The simple normality of the fractional powers of two and the Riemann zeta function', arXiv 2312.13943 (v1 21 Dec 2023; v2 29 Dec 2023). Abstract (as fetched, in summary): relates the frequency of the digit 1 in the binary expansion of 2^(p/q) to a mean value of the zeta function over arithmetic progressions; the zeta-weighted limit vanishes if and only if 2^(p/q) is simply normal to base 2. Later published as 'A criterion for the simple normality of fractional powers of two via the Riemann zeta function', Canad. J. Math., online 29 May 2025 (Cambridge page, search excerpt, not opened).
events.revisions: v1 21 Dec 2023; v2 29 Dec 2023. Journal version online 29 May 2025 (Canad. J. Math.); the first public written argument is the 2023 preprint.
events.delivers: An if-and-only-if criterion for simple normality to base 2 of the numbers 2^(p/q). For p/q in lowest terms with q > 1 these are irrational algebraic numbers. It is a criterion whose condition is not shown to hold for any p/q, so it establishes simple normality of no number.
events.remains: Whether the zeta condition holds for any 2^(p/q) (not decided here); every other algebraic irrational; every other base; full normality.

checked_by.who: Canadian Journal of Mathematics (Cambridge University Press)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper online on 29 May 2025 (per Cambridge page excerpt)

events.direction: A criterion, not an unconditional normality result. It cuts toward the conjecture only in the sense that it reduces one family's normality to an explicit limit.

events.what_happened: Pierpaolo Uberti, 'A note on normality of sqrt(2) in base 2', arXiv 1807.07338 (single version, 19 Jul 2018). Abstract as fetched in summary: assigns a vector to each number and reduces normality in base 2 to geometric properties of that vector; proves an infinite class of numbers is normal in base 2 and, as a further result, that sqrt(2) is normal in base 2. Only the abstract and metadata were read; the PDF was not.
events.delivers: Per the abstract, full normality of sqrt(2) in base 2 and of an infinite class of numbers in base 2. A single algebraic irrational in one base: a restricted case of the problem. Nothing in other bases.
events.remains: Every other base for sqrt(2); every other algebraic irrational; normality in some base or absolute normality in general.
events.doubts: No journal record and no third-party reading found. Only the arXiv page was read, not the proof.
events.direction: Claims a single-base, single-number case in favour of the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Yuya Kanado and Kota Saito, 'Normality of algebraic numbers and the Riemann zeta function', arXiv 2412.02337 (v1 3 Dec 2024; v2 17 Dec 2024). Shows: a positive algebraic irrational alpha is normal to base b if and only if, for every integer k >= 0, (1/log N) times the sum over 1 <= |n| <= N of zeta(-k + 2 pi i n / log b) e^(2 pi i n log alpha / log b) / n^(k+1) tends to 0. Introduction (verbatim): 'However, we do not get any examples of normal algebraic numbers.' Also quotes Borel's 1950 conjecture that all real algebraic irrational numbers are normal in any base at the same time.
events.revisions: v1 3 Dec 2024; v2 17 Dec 2024. What changed between versions was not checked.
events.delivers: An equivalence: normality to base b of each positive algebraic irrational is equivalent to an explicit zeta-function limit vanishing. It does not show any specific algebraic irrational normal, and the authors state that no examples are known.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no value of alpha is shown to satisfy the limit condition, so no algebraic irrational is shown normal in any base.
events.direction: A reformulation. It neither confirms nor refutes the conjecture; it changes the conjecture into a zeta-function identity that has not been verified for any alpha.

events.what_happened: Lucia Rossi, 'Digit expansions in rational and algebraic basis', arXiv 2505.14150 (single version, 20 May 2025). Introduces alpha-expansions of complex numbers in base alpha in Q(i) with |alpha| > 1, generalising rational base number systems; uniqueness almost everywhere; tilings; p-adic characterisation. Discarded: this is expansion in an algebraic base, not normality of algebraic reals in an integer base.
events.delivers: Expansion theory in bases alpha in Q(i) with |alpha| > 1, including uniqueness almost everywhere. It says nothing about the normality of algebraic irrationals in an integer base.

events.what_happened: Chokri Manai, 'Transcendence Meets Normality: Construction of Transcendentally Normal Numbers', arXiv 2508.09319 (v1 12 Aug 2025; v2 20 Oct 2025; v3 20 Aug 2026; v4 22 Sep 2026). Constructs numbers x for which p(x) is absolutely normal for every nonconstant integer polynomial p ('transcendentally normal'); proves almost every real is one; gives an explicit construction and an algorithm; extends to LIL-normal numbers. The introduction states Conjecture 1.4 (every irrational algebraic alpha is normal), says 'We are currently very far from proving Conjecture 1.4', and 'Most likely irrational algebraic numbers are normal for very different reasons than transcendent constants such as e and pi'. It records the bound that the number of 1s among the first N binary digits of an irrational algebraic number grows at least like sqrt(N), attributed to references [7] and [39] (the fetched text renders the exponent as 'N sqrt N'; read here as sqrt N).
events.revisions: v1 12 Aug 2025; v2 20 Oct 2025; v3 20 Aug 2026; v4 22 Sep 2026 (v4 comment: 'simplified and corrected proof, added references'). The v4 'AI Declaration' is recorded under ai.
events.delivers: Results about transcendentally normal numbers, a different class from algebraic irrationals (the property is required of p(x) for every polynomial p, and the class contains transcendental numbers). Nothing about the normality of any algebraic irrational.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; the paper restates Conjecture 1.4 as open.
events.doubts: A 2026 Manai paper, as seen in a search excerpt, lists this work as 'to appear in Proc. London Math. Soc.'. I did not verify that from the journal, and the arXiv page shows no journal reference.
events.direction: Not applicable to the algebraic question. The paper restates the conjecture as open and says the authors are far from proving it.

events.what_happened: Melodie Andrieu, Shalom Eliahou and Leo Vivion, 'A Normality Conjecture on Rational Base Number Systems', arXiv 2510.11723 (v1 6 Oct 2025; v2 7 Apr 2026). Conjecture (verbatim): 'every minimal and maximal word is normal over an appropriate subalphabet', for infinite words in rational base p/q; numerical support; implications for Mahler's Z-numbers, Flatto's Z_{p/q}-numbers and triple expansions. Presented as a seminar talk in Santiago in Jan 2026 (search excerpt).
events.revisions: v1 6 Oct 2025; v2 7 Apr 2026 (v2 is the current version).
events.delivers: Nothing proven. A conjecture about digit words in rational base systems, supported numerically. It is not about the normality of algebraic irrationals in integer bases.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different question, a conjecture about rational base systems.

events.what_happened: John M. Campbell, 'Abelian-normal decimal expansions', arXiv 2603.04396 (v1 4 Mar 2026; v2 21 Aug 2026). Defines abelian normality (counts over permutation classes of subwords, normalised); shows every normal number is abelian-normal; constructs a non-normal Champernowne-type constant D10 that is abelian-normal with respect to a weighting; asks whether a purely abelian-normal non-normal number exists. The v2 introduction and acknowledgements name GPT-5.6 Pro (see ai).
events.revisions: v1 4 Mar 2026; v2 21 Aug 2026. The AI credit appears in the v2 HTML; the v1 HTML read I did showed no AI mention, but that read covered only the theorem and open-problem sections (see incomplete).
events.delivers: An abelian-normal, non-normal constant D10 modelled on Champernowne's constant. It concerns decimal expansions of a transcendental-type construction, not algebraic numbers: the paper does not discuss whether D10 is algebraic (per the fetched text). It establishes nothing about the normality of algebraic irrationals.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different property (abelian normality) of a different number.

systems.name: GPT-5.6 Pro
systems.what_it_did: Per the author, used during the exploratory and proof-development stages. The introduction credits 'extensive interactions' with it for the explicit construction of a number that is abelian-normal but not normal (the paper's main example). The acknowledgements say all AI-generated suggestions were 'substantially revised, corrected, and independently verified by the author', who 'assumes full responsibility for the mathematical content'.
systems.basis_quote: The author acknowledges extensive interactions with GPT-5.6 Pro during the exploratory and proof-development stages

events.what_happened: google-deepmind/formal-conjectures issue #2256, 'Normality of Irrational Algebraic Numbers', opened 10 Feb 2026 by franzhusch. Asks whether all irrational algebraic numbers are normal in some base, 'Equivalently, are all irrational algebraic numbers absolutely normal?', and calls this 'an outstanding open problem in transcendental number theory'. Closed as completed on 11 Aug 2026 when PR #4624, 'feat(Wikipedia): separate algebraic normality conjectures' (opened 25 Jul 2026 by kernelpanic888, merged by mo271), split the two notions into distinct conjectures, defined irrational algebraic reals, and proved in Lean that absolute normality implies normality in base 2. The Lean file FormalConjectures/Wikipedia/AlgebraicNormality.lean states both conjectures with answer(sorry) placeholders and leaves their bodies as sorry; the lemma isNormalInBase_iff_isEquidistributedModuloOne also has a sorry body; only normal_in_some_base_of_absolutely_normal is proved.
events.revisions: Issue opened 10 Feb 2026; closed 11 Aug 2026 by PR #4624, which corrected the issue's equivalence and split the conjectures.
events.delivers: No new mathematics. A formal statement of two conjectures (absolute normality; normality in some base), a Lean definition of irrational algebraic reals, and the trivial implication absolute normality implies normality in base 2. The issue's claimed equivalence between the two notions was corrected by PR #4624.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including the question itself. The formal conjectures are unproven.

checked_by.qualification: Maintainer of the formal-conjectures repository. Not identified as a number theorist.
checked_by.what_they_did: Merged PR #4624 via the merge queue; the PR description states the file was checked with 'lake env lean'

events.doubts: The original issue asserted that normality in some base and absolute normality are equivalent for irrational algebraic numbers; PR #4624 calls this a false equivalence. The file contains sorry in the conjecture bodies and answer(sorry) placeholders, which is the repository's convention for open problems. The Lean file was read through a fetch summary, not as raw source.

withdrawn.what: The issue's claim that normality in some base and absolute normality are equivalent for irrational algebraic numbers, corrected by PR #4624 which separates the two conjectures.
withdrawn.by: other contributor (PR #4624 by kernelpanic888, merged by mo271)

events.direction: No direction: the entry makes no claim about whether any conjecture is true.

events.what_happened: Chokri Manai, 'On Normality Preserving Operations', arXiv 2609.24665 (single version, 21 Sep 2026). Per the abstract as fetched: the non-zero rationals are exactly the multiplicative normality-preserving numbers in a fixed integer base; extended to all bases using Hochman-Shmerkin; extends Rauzy's characterisation of additive normality preservation from normal to absolutely normal numbers; locally C^2 normality-preserving maps must be affine-linear, with a C^{1,1} counterexample.
events.delivers: Results on maps and operations that preserve normality. Nothing about the normality of any algebraic irrational. The fetched text does not mention algebraic irrationals.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different question about operations on normal numbers.

disputes.summary: Who posed the conjecture is stated inconsistently. Waldschmidt's 2009 survey abstract says Borel suggested in 1950 that the g-ary expansion of a real irrational algebraic number follows laws shared by almost all numbers. The Wikipedia article as fetched (last edited 2 Oct 2026) says 'it has also been conjectured' and cites Borel 1950 through a broken citation. A search excerpt of an older Wikipedia mirror credits Bailey and Crandall (2001), and the formal-conjectures issue cites Bailey and Crandall (2003). Recorded for the attribution pass; not a dispute about a result.

Three arXiv claims by one author (Isaac, 2005, 2011, 2013) and one by Uberti (2018) concern the normality in base 2 of square roots of non-squares or of sqrt(2). They overlap rather than conflict. MathWorld reports that some unnamed experts found the 2005 approach 'rather cloudy'. No journal publication or third-party acceptance of any of the four was found.

The formal-conjectures issue #2256 asserted that normality in some base and absolute normality are equivalent for irrational algebraic numbers. PR #4624 called this a false equivalence and split the two conjectures; the issue text was not edited to match.

summary: I ran 45 WebSearch queries (standard and extended) and about 35 WebFetch calls. Nothing I read reports any irrational algebraic number shown normal in any base, or any counterexample. The conjecture is stated as open in every 2024 to 2026 source I opened: Kanado and Saito (arXiv 2412.02337, Dec 2024; 'we do not get any examples of normal algebraic numbers'), Manai (arXiv 2508.09319, v1 Aug 2025 to v4 Sep 2026; 'We are currently very far from proving Conjecture 1.4'), the formal-conjectures issue (Feb 2026; 'an outstanding open problem'), and the Wikipedia 'Normal number' article (edited 2 Oct 2026; 'no irrational algebraic number has been proven to be normal in any base'). In-window events are: the Kanado-Saito criterion (an equivalence, no value shown normal); four neighbouring normal-number papers (Rossi 2025, Manai 2025, Andrieu et al. 2025, Campbell 2026) and one more (Manai 2026), all discounted as different questions; and the formal-conjectures issue, which has no new mathematics. Pre-window events are the 2004 and 2008 binary-count bounds (Bailey-Borwein-Crandall-Pomerance; Rivoal), the 2005 Adamczewski-Bugeaud complexity theorem, Kaneko 2010 digit changes, Nielsen-Simonsen 2013 numerics on 121 numbers, the Kanado-Saito 2023 criterion for 2^(p/q), and the Isaac 2005/2011/2013 and Uberti 2018 claims of base-2 normality for square roots and sqrt(2). Close calls: (i) the Isaac and Uberti claims are restricted cases (one base; simple normality for Isaac; one number for Uberti). Under the Wikipedia definition, normal means normal in all bases, so a single-base claim does not settle the bullet; under the reading 'normal in some base' it would settle a restricted part of it. Their correctness is unverified: MathWorld reports unnamed experts found the 2005 approach 'rather cloudy', and the 2005 v2 comment concedes an error in Lemma 6 of v1. (ii) Problem wording: the statement is ambiguous between normal in some base and absolutely normal; the formal-conjectures PR split these, and I have recorded both. (iii) AI involvement. No AI system is credited with any result on the normality of algebraic irrationals. Where AI appears in this neighbourhood: Campbell (2026) credits GPT-5.6 Pro in its v2 introduction and acknowledgements for the explicit construction in a paper about abelian normality, not algebraic numbers; Manai's v4 AI declaration (2508.09319) says an unnamed LLM was used to correct and streamline the Berry-Esseen argument in the proof of Proposition 4.4, a simplified definition of covers in section 4.3 and a more explicit Lemma 4.7, and that the original draft had no AI; Manai's 2609.24665 AI declaration says 'an LLM identified that a former proof for analytic maps can be generalized to C2-functions' (an idea used in the proof of Theorem 1.3), with the LLM unnamed; and the formal-conjectures issue was 'generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me' (agent unnamed), used for the statement only. None of these is a named system in the sense of section 5.4 for this problem, and none concerns algebraic irrationals. (iv) The Lean file contains sorry in the conjecture bodies and in one equivalence lemma, which is expected for open conjectures; the only proved theorem is the trivial base-2 implication.
competing_reading: The strongest case for counting something as progress is the Isaac and Uberti line. If one reads 'normal' as 'normal in some base' and takes the square-root and sqrt(2) claims at face value, the problem has a restricted settled part (sqrt(2) and sqrt(s) normal in base 2). The case against: the claims have had no third-party acceptance, the 2005 version was corrected once by its author, the 2013 version corrected its probability space in v5, and the problem's default reading (Wikipedia: normal in all bases) requires all bases at once, which no source claims. A second reading treats the Kanado-Saito criterion (2024) as real progress, because it recasts the conjecture as an explicit identity. The case against is that the identity is not shown to hold for any alpha, and the authors say no examples are known. A third reading treats Campbell's GPT-5.6 Pro credit as load-bearing AI involvement in normal-number mathematics. The case against is that the paper is not about algebraic numbers and the credit is in a paper outside this bullet's scope.
what_would_settle_it: For the Isaac and Uberti claims: a journal record, a published review, or a named expert's reading of the 2005 and 2013 proofs, or of Uberti's base-2 argument. For the bullet itself: a published or Lean-checked sorry-free proof that a named irrational algebraic number is normal in some base (or in every base). For the AI question on Campbell: the raw v1 PDF text, to confirm whether the GPT-5.6 Pro credit is absent in v1 as the HTML read suggests. For Manai 2025: a journal record for the Proc. London Math. Soc. publication claimed in a 2026 citation. For the formal-conjectures issue: nothing mathematical is needed; the question is only whether the repository's statement matches the reading the pass adopts.

judgement.why: No event shows any irrational algebraic number normal in any base. Post-snapshot: the Kanado-Saito 2024 equivalence is a reformulation (none); Rossi, Manai (both), Andrieu et al. and Campbell address different questions (variant); the formal-conjectures entry is a formal statement with no new mathematics (none). Pre-snapshot: digit-count, digit-change and complexity bounds concern quantities other than normality (variant); Nielsen-Simonsen is finite numerics (instances); Isaac's claims are simple normality only, a weaker property (variant), and doubtful. The close call is Uberti 2018: a single number in a single base is at most a case, but a landmark claim with no uptake in eight years, contradicted by every later source still calling the question open, is set aside as not_credible. Campbell's GPT-5.6 Pro credit for the explicit construction is assisted for that event, but the event is a variant.
judgement.doubts: Campbell's AI credit comes from a fetch summary of v2 and may postdate v1; immaterial since the event is a variant. Uberti not_credible rests on silence plus contradicting later statements, not on an identified error.
